title: Cranial Nerve VII (The Facial Nerve)
subtitle: Tell central from peripheral facial palsy, then place a peripheral lesion by taste, hearing and tearing

points.text: The facial motor nucleus sits in the caudal pontine tegmentum, dorsal to the superior olive.
points.quote: Fibers of the motor division arise from the facial motor nucleus, located in the ventrolateral caudal pontine tegmentum, dorsal to the superior olive

points.text: The intrapontine fascicle loops around the abducens nucleus as the genu, which is why pontine lesions can involve both CN VI and CN VII.
points.quote: These roots then sweep from medial to lateral around the dorsal surface of the abducens nucleus as the genu of the facial nerve

points.text: Voluntary facial movement is driven by corticobulbar fibers from the lower precentral gyrus.
points.quote: Supranuclear control of facial movements is mediated through corticobulbar fibers originating from the lower third of the precentral gyrus.

points.text: The part of the nucleus supplying the upper face has bilateral supranuclear control, so a supranuclear lesion spares the forehead.
points.quote: supplying the upper muscles of facial expression such as the frontalis and orbicularis oculi, is spared due to its bilateral supranuclear control

points.text: Emotional (involuntary) facial movement uses a separate pathway that does not run in the internal capsule.
points.quote: Fibers mediating emotional facial movements do not descend within the internal capsule in their course to the facial motor nuclei.

points.text: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the nervus intermedius, a thinner nerve than the motor root.
points.quote: Taste sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by a thinner nerve, the nervus intermedius of Wrisberg

points.text: The greater superficial petrosal nerve arises at the geniculate ganglion and carries parasympathetic fibers for tearing.
points.quote: arising from the apex of the geniculate ganglion, is composed of preganglionic parasympathetic efferents innervating the lacrimal, palatal, and nasal glands

points.text: In the mastoid segment the stapedius nerve branches off first, then the chorda tympani, which joins the lingual nerve.
points.quote: the nerve to the stapedius muscle originates near the upper end, and the other branch, the chorda tympani, joins the lingual nerve

points.text: The chorda tympani also carries taste afferents toward the nucleus tractus solitarius.
points.quote: The chorda tympani also contains afferent taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue destined for the nucleus tractus solitarius.

points.text: The intracranial segment of the nerve is supplied by AICA.
points.quote: The intracranial segment of the facial nerve receives its blood supply from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA)

coreAnatomy.title: Bedside tests that place the lesion

points.text: Taste, hyperacusis and tearing each point to a different branch, so together they locate the lesion along the nerve.
points.quote: The lesion site can be deduced by assessing whether there is preservation or impairment of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani),

points.text: Stapedius involvement makes low tones sound louder on the affected side.
points.quote: Hyperacusis resulting from stapedius muscle involvement is more notable for low tones that sound louder on the affected side.

points.text: The facial nerve is the efferent limb of the corneal and palpebral reflexes, which are depressed on the side of a lower motor neuron lesion.
points.quote: The facial nerve is the efferent limb of the corneal and palpebral reflexes, which are ipsilaterally depressed with lower motor neuron

localizationRules.explanation: Contralateral weakness of voluntary facial movement with relative sparing of forehead and orbicularis oculi; the mouth region is most affected.
localizationRules.quote: there is paresis of voluntary movements of the muscles of facial expression contralateral to the affected hemisphere, with relative sparing of the frontalis and orbicularis oculi

localizationRules.rule: Nuclear or fascicular lesion = peripheral palsy
localizationRules.explanation: A complete pontine lesion of the nucleus or fascicle gives an ipsilateral palsy of the whole face, including the forehead, so look for neighbouring pontine signs.
localizationRules.quote: With complete lesions, there is unilateral ipsilateral paralysis of all mimetic facial muscles, with loss of frontal wrinkling

localizationRules.explanation: CN VII is next to the nervus intermedius and CN VIII there, so expect facial weakness with impaired taste plus ipsilateral tinnitus, deafness and vertigo, and look for pons, cerebellar and trigeminal signs.
localizationRules.quote: Cerebellopontine angle lesions frequently involve neighboring structures, including the pons (nystagmus or ipsilateral gaze palsy), cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum (ipsilateral ataxia)

localizationRules.rule: Lesion in the facial canal: tearing
localizationRules.explanation: Whether tearing is impaired tells you if the lesion is proximal or distal to the greater superficial petrosal nerve.
localizationRules.quote: With lesions proximal to the greater superficial petrosal nerve, lacrimation is impaired; with distal lesions, lacrimation is normal.

localizationRules.rule: Lesion after the stapedius and chorda tympani
localizationRules.explanation: Between the stapedius branch and the chorda tympani, taste is lost but hearing is spared; distal to the chorda tympani only the motor palsy remains.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions in this segment result in peripheral facial paralysis without hyperacusis or impaired taste.

keySyndromes.name: Millard-Gubler syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Ipsilateral lateral rectus paralysis + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Ventral pontine lesion that includes the corticospinal tract; compare with Foville, where the gaze center is involved instead of the lateral rectus.
keySyndromes.quote: results from ventral pontine lesions interrupting the fascicles of the facial and abducens nerves and the corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Foville syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Paralysis of conjugate gaze to the side of the lesion + Contralateral hemiplegia
keySyndromes.clue: Pontine tegmental lesion involving the PPRF, so the gaze palsy is conjugate toward the lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: The Foville syndrome results from pontine tegmental lesions interrupting the fascicles of the facial nerve, the PPRF, and the corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Eight-and-a-half syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) plus horizontal gaze palsy + Ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy
keySyndromes.clue: One-and-a-half syndrome plus ipsilateral facial palsy from a dorsal caudal pontine tegmental lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: The eight-and-a-half syndrome results from dorsal tegmental caudal pontine lesions involving the PPRF or the abducens nucleus, the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)

keySyndromes.name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion)
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral peripheral facial paralysis + Hyperacusis + Impaired taste + Geniculate neuralgia + Herpetic vesicles of eardrum, external auditory meatus or palate
keySyndromes.clue: Reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion; the book notes that some cases occur without a rash (zoster sine herpete).
keySyndromes.quote: hyperacusis, impaired taste, geniculate neuralgia, and herpetic vesicles involving the eardrum, external auditory meatus, or palate

keySyndromes.name: Bell palsy
keySyndromes.triad: Acute onset + Unilateral lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial muscles + Often preceded by ear pain, dysgeusia, hyperacusis or decreased tearing
keySyndromes.clue: Idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion; the book gives red flags (for example gradual progression beyond 3 weeks) that point elsewhere.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a common (up to 40/100,000) acute monosymptomatic, idiopathic, unilateral, lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial muscles

keySyndromes.name: Hemifacial spasm
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral intermittent involuntary spasms + Usually start in orbicularis oculi and spread to other ipsilateral facial muscles + Often a vascular loop at the root exit zone
keySyndromes.clue: A hyperactive, not weak, facial nerve; compression at the root exit zone in the cerebellopontine angle is the most common cause.
keySyndromes.quote: unilateral, intermittent, involuntary, hyperactive dysfunction of the seventh CN, most commonly due to a vascular loop abutting the facial nerve at the root exit zone

boardTraps.text: Voluntary and emotional facial movements can dissociate: voluntary paresis without emotional paresis is the far more common pattern after corticobulbar interruption.
boardTraps.quote: Volitional facial paresis without emotional is far more common than emotional facial paresis and results from interruption of corticobulbar pathways

boardTraps.text: The Bell phenomenon (eye rolling up and out on attempted closure) is a normal response that only becomes visible when the eyelid cannot close.
boardTraps.quote: The Bell phenomenon represents a normal response that becomes apparent due to paralysis of eyelid closure.

boardTraps.text: Not every peripheral facial palsy is Bell palsy, even though that is the most common cause; check the red-flag list before labeling it idiopathic.
boardTraps.quote: Bell palsy is by far the most common cause of unilateral peripheral facial nerve paralysis, not every peripheral facial palsy is the result of Bell palsy

boardTraps.text: A brainstem lesion can cause facial paresis with taste and tearing preserved, because the motor fibers are anatomically separate from the sensory-parasympathetic components.
boardTraps.quote: brainstem lesions may produce facial paresis with sparing of taste and tearing due to the anatomic separation of the motor fibers from the sensory-parasympathetic components

boardTraps.text: Aberrant regeneration after a peripheral palsy can cause crocodile tears (Bogorad syndrome) on the paretic side.
boardTraps.quote: aberrant regeneration may result in involuntary tearing of the eye on the involved paretic side (crocodile-tears or Bogorad syndrome)

boardTraps.text: In facial palsy, resting upper eyelid position and gentle closure are unaffected; blinking and tight closure are what fail.
boardTraps.quote: in cases of facial nerve palsy, the position of the upper eyelid, gentle closure of the eye, and lid-eye coordination are unaffected
